recognition.practicalTip: When identifying Greek verbal forms, first look for the ending to determine person and number, then the temporal stem for tense, and finally analyze prefixes (augment, reduplication) to confirm aspect.
recognition.attentionText: Some forms are visually similar but function differently. Pay special attention to syntactic context to distinguish between forms that share identical endings.

function.semanticText: This word's syntactic function is not merely grammatical – it directly affects the theological meaning of the passage. Consider how this construction directs the reader's attention to certain aspects of the divine message.
function.pulpitTip: When preaching, help your congregation see how the grammatical structure reveals the inspired author's intention. Syntax is theology in action.

onboarding.intro: This tool helps you understand the Greek text structure before studying individual words.
onboarding.steps: I'll show you the key elements in 5 quick steps.

onboarding.step1Content: Read this blue box first. It gives you the full picture of the passage's argument.
onboarding.step2Content1: Clauses with blue background are the main ones - the backbone of the text.

onboarding.step3Content1: Indented clauses depend on the main one.
onboarding.step3Content2: The color tells you its function: green (purpose), orange (cause), etc.

onboarding.step5Content1: Each color represents a clause type with a specific function.
onboarding.step5Content2: For example: Green = Purpose ("so that..."), Orange = Cause ("because...")

clues.title: Recognition clues
clues.source: Analysis: MorphGNT (word-by-word academic review). The clues point at the marks in the form that confirm it.
clues.infPresActive: The ending {{marker}} marks the present active infinitive.
clues.infPresMedio: The ending {{marker}} marks the present middle/passive infinitive.
clues.infAorActive: The ending {{marker}} marks the aorist active infinitive.
clues.infAorMedio: The ending {{marker}} marks the aorist middle infinitive.
clues.infAorPasivo: The ending {{marker}} marks the aorist passive infinitive.
clues.infPerfActive: The ending {{marker}} marks the perfect active infinitive.
clues.aoristoSigmatico: The suffix {{marker}} is the signature of the (first) sigmatic aorist.
clues.aoristoPasivo: The suffix {{marker}} marks the aorist passive.
clues.futuroSigma: The {{marker}} added to the stem marks the future.
clues.reduplicacion: The initial reduplication ({{marker}}) marks the perfect.
clues.perfectoKappa: The {{marker}} before the ending marks the perfect active.
clues.aumento: The augment {{marker}} at the start signals a secondary (past) tense in the indicative.
clues.impvActPl: The ending {{marker}} marks the active imperative, 2nd plural.
clues.impvMedPl: The ending {{marker}} marks the middle imperative, 2nd plural.
clues.subjuntivoVocalLarga: The lengthened theme vowel ({{marker}}) is the signature of the subjunctive.
clues.participioMedio: The infix {{marker}} marks the middle/passive participle.
clues.participioActivo: The marks {{marker}} signal the active participle.
clues.participioAorAct: The marks {{marker}} signal the aorist active participle.
clues.articleParadigm: The article {{marker}} belongs to the paradigm memorized first: it gives away case, number and gender of its whole phrase.
clues.iotaSubscript: The iota subscript ({{marker}}) is the classic mark of the dative singular.
clues.nomSgOs: The ending {{marker}} marks the nominative singular masculine (2nd declension).
clues.genSgOu: The ending {{marker}} marks the genitive singular (2nd declension).
clues.genSg1: The ending {{marker}} marks the genitive singular (1st declension).
clues.genPlOn: The ending {{marker}} marks the genitive plural — in ALL declensions.
clues.datPl: The ending {{marker}} marks the dative plural (1st/2nd declension).
clues.accSgN: The ending {{marker}} marks the accusative singular.
clues.accPl: The ending {{marker}} marks the accusative plural.
clues.nomPl: The ending {{marker}} marks the nominative plural.
clues.postpositive: The particle {{marker}} is POSTPOSITIVE: it never opens its clause, sitting second even though it links the whole sentence to what precedes. Spanish and English translate it first, which hides the clue.

analyzer.literalHint: (mirrors the Greek word order — compare it with the fluid one)
analyzer.wordOrderRule: Greek marks function with CASES, not order — so its order is free and used for emphasis. Spanish depends on order, so translation reorders.

bridge.bridgeGenitive: The "of" is not in the Greek: the genitive case carries it inside — it does the preposition’s job.
bridge.bridgeDative: The "to/for/in" is not in the Greek: the dative case carries it inside.
bridge.bridgeAccusative: The accusative marks the direct object — Spanish needs no preposition, only position.
bridge.bridgeNominative: The nominative is the case of the subject and of what is said about it (predicates and appositions) — regardless of its position in the sentence.
bridge.bridgeVocative: The vocative is the case of direct address: Spanish marks it with commas.

caseFnHint.subject: Performs the action of the finite verb.
caseFnHint.predicateNominative: States WHAT the subject is (with "to be").
caseFnHint.absolute: Headings, titles and letter salutations: depends on no finite verb.
caseFnHint.appellation: The name itself, not what is said about it.
caseFnHint.apposition: The genitive IS what it specifies.
caseFnHint.pendent: Stated first; the sentence then goes another way.
caseFnHint.subjective: The genitive ACTS ("the love of God" = God loves).
caseFnHint.objective: The genitive RECEIVES ("the fear of God" = God is feared).
caseFnHint.attributive: Works like an adjective ("body of sin" = sinful body).
caseFnHint.partitive: The WHOLE from which a part is taken.
caseFnHint.objectOfPreposition: The case is required by the preceding preposition.
caseFnHint.indirectObject: To whom the action is directed.
caseFnHint.reference: "With respect to", the frame of the claim.
caseFnHint.sphere: The realm in which something holds.
caseFnHint.subjectOfInfinitive: Acts as subject inside an infinitive clause.

rhetoric.disclaimer: Rhetorical structure is a READING of the text, not manuscript data — unlike morphology. Chiasms are often over-diagnosed: judge it yourself.

articleUseHint.anaphoric: Picks up something already mentioned: "THAT very thing I just named". This is why a verse can open with an article.
articleUseHint.deictic: Points at something present in the scene.
articleUseHint.parExcellence: The one of its class par excellence (the Prophet, the Christ).
articleUseHint.monadic: The only one of its kind (the sun, the devil).
articleUseHint.wellKnown: The one everyone knows, even if unmentioned before.
articleUseHint.generic: The whole class, not an individual.
articleUseHint.abstract: Goes with a quality and makes it concrete (the faith, the love).
articleUseHint.possessive: Acts as a possessive: "he raised THE hand" = his hand.
articleUseHint.substantivizer: Turns an infinitive, adjective or whole phrase into a noun.
articleUseHint.withProperName: With a proper name: familiarity, or picking someone up again.

composition.title: Compound word
composition.rootFallacy: Careful: this word’s actual usage is NOT the sum of its parts. Preaching its etymology would claim something the text does not say.

discourseHint.development: A NEW step in the argument, not necessarily contrary. δέ is this — always translating it "but" invents an opposition that is not there.
discourseHint.contrast: Genuinely opposes what follows to what precedes.
discourseHint.correction: Corrects or replaces what was just said.
discourseHint.pointCounterpoint: Announces a pair: the first is said expecting the second (μέν… δέ).
discourseHint.resumption: Picks up a thread left earlier.
discourseHint.condition: States the condition the rest depends on.
